question: A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation from a flood-affected area presents with acute jaundice. Anti-HAV IgM is negative. Which test should be ordered next, and why?

answers.text: Anti-HEV IgM — HEV genotype 1 causes waterborne epidemic hepatitis with 20–25% maternal fatality in third trimester

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In flood/outbreak settings in India, HEV genotype 1 is the leading cause of epidemic jaundice. Its 20–25% case fatality rate in third-trimester pregnancy — the highest of any viral hepatitis — makes urgent anti-HEV IgM testing critical for prognostication and intensive monitoring.

answers.text: HBsAg — HBV is the commonest cause of jaundice in pregnancy in India

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HBV is parenterally transmitted, not waterborne. While HBsAg screening is routine in pregnancy, the flood-affected setting with an outbreak pattern strongly suggests faeco-oral transmission — pointing to HEV rather than HBV.

answers.text: HCV RNA — HCV is the commonest cause of waterborne hepatitis outbreaks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HCV is transmitted parenterally (IV drug use, unsafe injections, transfusions). It is NOT waterborne and does not cause epidemic outbreaks. This is a common factual error in examinations.

answers.text: Anti-HAV IgG — to confirm past immunity to hepatitis A

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anti-HAV IgG tests for past immunity, not acute disease. Moreover, acute HAV has already been excluded here (IgM negative), so IgG adds no diagnostic value.

overallFeedback.feedback: Flood + outbreak + pregnancy + HAV excluded → think HEV genotype 1. Critical because of 20–25% third-trimester fatality. Test: anti-HEV IgM.
HEV in pregnancy (third trimester) = 20–25% fatality. In Indian flood outbreaks, always test anti-HEV IgM when HAV is excluded.
